Carousing is a way for you to convert the coin you've earned into XP and other benefits.
You'll likely come out of a carousing event with a new NPC contact, whether friend or foe. You might even acquire a new magic item if you're bold and lucky enough.

Learning

In order to learn a new skill, you must find a capable instructor who is willing to teach you.

In smoky gambling dens, raucous taverns, and dim back alleys, the clatter of dice signals a game of Wizards and Thieves.
Wizards and Thieves is a fast-paced betting game beloved by gamblers of all stripes. Use it when you want to play out a wager using a quick system.
To Start
To begin, the players agree to a number of coins each will bring to the game (typically 20). Each player adds 6 coins to the pot.
All players roll 3d6. The player with the highest result becomes the **active player**. Gameplay moves clockwise from that person.

Rolls of **wizards** (6s) and **thieves** (1s) **cancel** each other out on a one-to-one basis when determining majorities. **Ignore** results of 1 and 6 when adding to or taking from the pot unless no other die type remains.
Gameplay
The active player declares *wizard* or *thief* before rolling 3d6.
**Declared thief, rolled majority**
**thieves:** The active player takes coins from the pot equal to the lowest remaining die after cancellations/ignores. The active player goes again.
**Declared thief, rolled majority**
**wizards:** The active player adds coins to the pot equal to the lowest remaining die after cancellations/ignores. Play passes to the next player.
**Declared wizard, rolled majority**
**wizards:** Everyone but the active player adds coins to the pot equal to the lowest remaining die after cancellations/ignores. The active player goes again.
**Declared wizard, rolled majority**
**thieves:** The active player adds coins to the pot equal to the lowest remaining die after cancellations/ignores. Play passes to the next player.
**No wizard or thief majority:** Play passes to the next player.
**Rolled 3 wizards:** The active player takes the whole pot. The game ends.

**Rolled 3 thieves:** The pot is split evenly among all the remaining players except the active player. The active player gets any remainder that doesn’t divide evenly, a result called “honor among thieves.” The game ends.
The Game Ends
The game ends when the pot reaches 0.
If a player runs out of coins, that player is out of the game.
If all but one player loses their last coin, the pot goes to the player whose turn it would have been after the last roll.
The game's winner is the person who ends with the most coins.
A character's **renown** can grow over time and increase their fame (or infamy). Having a high renown confers benefits.
Renown
A PC's renown starts out being equal to their CHA modifier (it can be negative).
**3 or Less.** You're mostly invisible, even to regular folks. You're not welcome in upscale places.
**4-7.** Gain a **+1 renown bonus** on carousing event rolls. Regular folk view you favorably. People of high status ignore you, especially in upscale places.
**8-11.** Gain a **+2 renown bonus** on carousing event rolls. You're a known name. High-status people treat you as a peer.
**12+.** Gain a **+3 renown bonus** on carousing event rolls. You're a celebrity, welcome in the most luxurious of places. People of high status defer to you.
Gaining Renown
PCs gain a point of renown each time the following occurs:
Gaining a level
Being honored publicly
Extravagant public spending
A major triumph or success
Losing Renown
PCs lose a point of renown each time the following occurs:
Public humiliation
A negative run-in with the law
Committing a fashion mistake
Making a cultural faux pas
Offending a person of higher renown or social status
Reactions
PCs may add their renown bonus to their **reaction rolls** when they are in a location where they are likely to be recognized. Double 1s always result in a hostile reaction.

In a West Marches campaign, there are two primary options for how you can track the passage of time. Some methods are better suited for different groups and play styles.
Fixed Time
With a fixed time campaign, the GM manually tracks the passage of time as the PCs undertake activities and rests.
This method is how most GMs track time. It works well with 2-7 players who regularly attend each session and who prefer to develop one character each.
In fixed-time play, the game world "freezes" between sessions, and the PCs play out downtime during sessions.
Using fixed time makes it easy to skip forward in time when needed, and many GMs use the standard rest and healing rules in *Shadowdark RPG* core when tracking time this way.
Real Time
A popular technique from the early days of fantasy TTRPGs was to sync the passage of in-game time with the passage of real-world time (known as **1:1 time**).
This method works well for large groups of players (8+) who do not attend every session and who like the idea of developing multiple characters each.
Days, seasons, and even years move along with the outside world. It's simple to track but introduces a few considerations.

**Between Games.** The players can use the real-world time between sessions to undertake downtime events or overland travel. It's important to note how long these activities take. See **Frozen PCs** for more details.
**Healing.** Using a slow healing mode, such as **Grinder Mode** (*Shadowdark RPG* pg. 111) enhances the impact of tracking the game's progress in real time.
**Frozen PCs.** Characters whose game world activities take up long spans of time are "frozen in action" until the real world catches up with them.
For instance, a character who spends a week traveling to, exploring, and returning from a dungeon during a game session becomes unavailable to play for seven days of real-world time.

Likewise, a PC who spends their downtime between sessions carousing for two days becomes unavailable for two days of real-world time. While it's likely this PC will be available again by the next game session, it still places a limit on how much they can do during their downtime.
If an event **disrupts** a character's progress while frozen, such as a random encounter, the GM and player should resolve the event. The player may then resume or revise their PC's actions.
**Multiple PCs.** Because PCs can become frozen in time, it's essential for players to have alternate characters to pilot during sessions and downtime.
1:1 Downtime
If you are using real time to track your game, you'll need to determine how long downtime activities take.
**Carousing.** As a rule of thumb, PCs should only be permitted to carouse once every two weeks of real time. This prevents PCs from carousing too frequently per Shadowdark's intended rules.
Unless otherwise noted, a carousing session takes as many days at the carousing event bonus (minimum 1 day).
**Learning.** Unless otherwise noted, all learning attempts take 2d6 days to complete.
**Other Activities.** Spell research, rumor mongering, criminal activities, meditation, or getting locked up in the city jail can all last for variable amounts of time given the situation.
There may be an obvious ruling for how long an activity takes, but when in doubt, assume it takes 2d6 days.

Farkle is a two-player dice game that can be enjoyed in most taverns. The standard wager is 3 gp, but experienced gamblers may want to put more at stake. Be aware that the dice are fickle, and you can easily lose great sums in a moment of bad luck.
Each player rolls six dice and whoever has the highest total goes first. From that point on, players then alternate turns.
The active player rolls all six dice. They must then choose to score one or more dice (based on the criteria below).
Scoring:
is worth 10 points.
is worth 5 points.
Three of a kind is worth 10 x the number shown. Three 3s would be worth 30 points.
Four of a kind is worth double that value. Making four 3s worth 60 points (30 x 2).
Five of a kind is worth double again. Making five 3s worth 120 points (60 x 2).
If a player cannot score using any of the dice rolled (a bust), their turn ends. Play passes to the other player and no points are saved that round.
Decision Point:
After scoring, the player must choose to either stay or press their luck.
If they stay, the points scored on this turn are recorded and saved. If this gives them 250+ points, they win the game. If not, play passes to the other player.
If they press their luck, they can collect the unscored dice and re-roll them. If all dice were just scored, they can make this re-roll with a full set of six dice.

However, if the player busts while pressing their luck, all points rolled previously on that turn will be lost. The player must evaluate whether pressing their luck is a worthwhile strategy. The game can be won by slowly building up saved points or blitzing forward with a few high-scoring rolls.
